questions.question: Q: How many declensions are there in Latin?

points.text: Five: first (a-stem), second (o-stem), third (consonant/i-stem), fourth (u-stem), and fifth (e-stem).

questions.question: Q: What gender are most first declension nouns? Name two masculine exceptions.

points.text: Mostly feminine. Masculine exceptions include nauta (sailor) and agricola (farmer).

questions.question: Q: How do you find the stem of a third declension noun?

points.text: Remove the genitive singular ending (-is) from the genitive form. For example: rex, regis → stem is reg-.

questions.question: Q: What is the special rule for neuter nouns?

points.text: The nominative and accusative are always identical in both singular and plural. The plural nominative/accusative ending is -a.

questions.question: Q: Give an example of a fourth declension noun and a fifth declension noun.

points.text: Fourth declension: adventus (arrival, masculine). Fifth declension: res (thing, feminine) or dies (day, feminine/masculine).

questions.question: Q: Why must you learn the gender of a Latin noun?

points.text: Gender determines which adjective endings and pronouns agree with the noun. It cannot always be predicted from the declension and must be memorised.

questions.question: Q: What is the difference between consonant stems and i-stems in the third declension?

points.text: I-stems have -ium in the genitive plural and -ia in the neuter nominative/accusative plural. Consonant stems have -um in the genitive plural and -a in the neuter plural. I-stems also show -im in the accusative singular for some nouns.
